prompt: A platform team decides to treat its internal developer platform as a product. What does this primarily mean in practice?
options: Treating application developers as customers: doing user research, maintaining a roadmap, and measuring adoption and satisfaction
Selling access to the platform to external companies to recover its cost
Building every capability developers might one day ask for before onboarding the first team
Mandating that all teams use the platform through an executive decree
optionNotes: Correct. Platform as a product means the platform team has internal customers, gathers their needs, prioritises a roadmap, ships iteratively, and tracks adoption and satisfaction just like a product team.
Platform as a product is about product thinking, not commercial resale; the platform serves internal teams.
Building everything up front is the opposite of product thinking, which favours a thin, iterative platform driven by real demand.
Mandated adoption is a common anti-pattern; a product-minded platform earns adoption by being the easiest path, not by decree.
explanation: The CNCF Platforms white paper and Team Topologies both frame the platform as an internal product with developers as its customers. That implies user research, a prioritised roadmap, iterative delivery and measurement of adoption and satisfaction. Reselling, big-bang building or mandated use all miss the point.
example:
# a lightweight platform product backlog
- [ ] interview 5 app teams on onboarding pain
- [ ] ship golden path: 'new-service' template (v0.1)
- [ ] measure: time-to-first-deploy, weekly active teams
- [ ] quarterly NPS survey to platform users
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["App teams as customers"] -->|"needs and feedback"| R["Platform roadmap"]
    R --> S["Ship increment"]
    S --> M["Measure adoption and satisfaction"]
    M -->|"learn"| U

prompt: In platform engineering, what is a golden path (also called a paved road)?
options: An opinionated, supported, self-service route to build and run a common type of workload, which teams may still deviate from
A mandatory architecture that every team must follow without exception
The production network path with the lowest latency between two clusters
A checklist that security signs off before any release
optionNotes: Correct. A golden path is a well-supported, opinionated default (templates, pipelines, runtime config) that makes the recommended way the easiest way, while still allowing teams to leave the path when they have a real need.
Golden paths are opt-in and supported, not enforced mandates; that is what distinguishes them from a rigid standard.
This describes network routing, unrelated to the developer-experience concept.
A release checklist is a governance gate, not a self-service delivery path.
explanation: Golden paths (Spotify's term) or paved roads (Netflix's term) are opinionated, self-service, supported defaults for common tasks such as creating a new microservice. They reduce cognitive load by making the right thing the easy thing, but they are not mandates: teams can go off-road and accept more responsibility.
example:
# Backstage software template exposing a golden path
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: go-service
spec:
  steps:
  - id: fetch
    action: fetch:template   # repo skeleton with CI, Helm chart, SLOs
  - id: publish
    action: publish:github
diagram:
flowchart LR
    DEV["Developer"] -->|"self-service"| GP["Golden path template"]
    GP --> REPO["Repo with CI pipeline"]
    GP --> CHART["Helm chart and runtime defaults"]
    GP --> OBS["Dashboards and SLOs"]
    DEV -.->|"may go off-road"| CUSTOM["Custom setup, more ownership"]

prompt: According to Team Topologies, the primary purpose of a platform team is to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned (product) teams so they can deliver faster.
explanation: Team Topologies defines the platform team as one that provides internal services to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams, letting them focus on their business domain. The platform is consumed via an X-as-a-Service interaction mode rather than a ticket-driven hand-off.

# Team Topologies interaction modes
stream-aligned team  --X-as-a-Service-->  platform team
stream-aligned team  --collaboration---->  enabling team (temporary)
# goal: stream-aligned teams own build+run without carrying all infra knowledge

    SA2["Stream-aligned team B"] -->|"consumes as a service"| PT
    PT --> CL["Lower cognitive load for product teams"]
    EN["Enabling team"] -.->|"temporary collaboration"| SA1

prompt: The CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model defines four maturity levels: Provisional, Operational, Scalable and one more. Name the highest level.
explanation: The CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model describes progression across five aspects (Investment, Adoption, Interfaces, Operations, Measurement) through four levels: Provisional, Operational, Scalable and Optimizing. At the Optimizing level the platform is continuously improved based on quantitative feedback and is treated fully as a product.
example:
# Maturity model summary
Aspects: Investment | Adoption | Interfaces | Operations | Measurement
Levels : 1 Provisional -> 2 Operational -> 3 Scalable -> 4 Optimizing
diagram:
flowchart LR
    L1["1 Provisional"] --> L2["2 Operational"]
    L2 --> L3["3 Scalable"]
    L3 --> L4["4 Optimizing"]
    A["Aspects: investment, adoption, interfaces, operations, measurement"] -.-> L1

prompt: What is the conventional file name, placed in a repository root, that Backstage reads to register a Component or other entity in its Software Catalog?
explanation: Backstage discovers catalog entities from `catalog-info.yaml` descriptor files, typically at the root of a repository. The file uses the `backstage.io/v1alpha1` API and declares kinds such as Component, API, System or Resource together with ownership and relations.
example:
# catalog-info.yaml
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: acme/payments-api
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-payments
diagram:
flowchart LR
    REPO["Git repo with catalog-info.yaml"] -->|"discovery or manual register"| CAT["Backstage catalog processor"]
    CAT --> ENT["Component entity"]
    ENT --> OWN["owner: team-payments"]
    ENT --> UI["Portal page with TechDocs, CI, K8s plugins"]

prompt: A platform team wants to report the four DORA key metrics for teams using its golden paths. Which metrics belong to that set? (Select all that apply.)
options: Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Time to restore service
Code coverage percentage
Number of pull requests merged per developer
optionNotes: Deployment frequency (how often code reaches production) is one of the four DORA key metrics.
Lead time for changes (commit to running in production) is a DORA key metric.
Change failure rate (share of deployments causing an incident or rollback) is a DORA key metric.
Time to restore service (MTTR after a production failure) is a DORA key metric.
Code coverage is a testing-quality signal, not one of the DORA metrics.
PR counts per developer are an output/activity metric that DORA research explicitly avoids because it encourages gaming.
explanation: The DORA research program identifies four key metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service (a fifth, reliability, was added later). They measure throughput and stability of delivery, which is why platform teams use them to show the platform's impact. Coverage and per-developer PR counts are not part of the set.
example:
# PromQL-style sketches feeding a DORA dashboard
sum(increase(deployments_total{env="prod"}[7d]))          # deployment frequency
histogram_quantile(0.5, commit_to_deploy_seconds_bucket)   # lead time
sum(failed_deploys_total) / sum(deployments_total)         # change failure rate
avg(incident_restore_seconds)                              # time to restore
diagram:
flowchart LR
    T["Throughput"] --> DF["Deployment frequency"]
    T --> LT["Lead time for changes"]
    S["Stability"] --> CFR["Change failure rate"]
    S --> TTR["Time to restore"]
    P["Platform golden path"] -->|"improves"| T
    P -->|"improves"| S

prompt: A platform team ships a base set of Kubernetes manifests and wants application teams to customise them per environment by applying patches, without introducing a templating language. Which tool fits this requirement best?
options: Kustomize
Helm
Terraform
Crossplane
optionNotes: Correct. Kustomize is template-free: it layers overlays and strategic-merge or JSON patches on top of a base, which is exactly patch-based customisation.
Helm uses Go templating with values files; it is a packaging and templating tool rather than a patch-based one.
Terraform is a general infrastructure-as-code tool with its own HCL language; it is not designed for patching Kubernetes manifests.
Crossplane composes cloud infrastructure via Kubernetes APIs; it is not a manifest customisation tool.
explanation: Kustomize (built into `kubectl -k`) customises raw YAML through bases and overlays using patches, so no templating is needed. Helm is the templating/packaging option; Terraform and Crossplane target infrastructure provisioning rather than manifest customisation.
example:
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
- ../../base
patches:
- path: replicas.yaml   # bump replicas only in prod
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
diagram:
flowchart LR
    B["base manifests"] --> O1["overlay dev"]
    B --> O2["overlay prod"]
    O2 -->|"patch replicas, image tag"| R["rendered YAML"]
    R -->|"kubectl apply -k"| K["Cluster"]

prompt: A platform team introduces a Kyverno `ClusterPolicy` that requires every Pod to set resource limits. During rollout they want violations to be reported without blocking any deployments. Which setting achieves this?
options: `validationFailureAction: Audit`
`validationFailureAction: Enforce`
`background: false`
`failurePolicy: Ignore`
optionNotes: Correct. With `Audit`, Kyverno records violations as PolicyReports (and events) but still admits the resource, which is the standard way to roll a policy out safely.
`Enforce` rejects non-compliant resources at admission time, which would block deployments.
`background` controls whether existing resources are scanned; it does not change admission behaviour.
`failurePolicy` governs what the API server does if the webhook itself is unavailable, not how policy violations are handled.
explanation: Kyverno validation rules have `validationFailureAction` set to `Audit` or `Enforce`. Audit mode admits the resource and writes a PolicyReport so teams can see what would fail, while Enforce blocks it. `background` and `failurePolicy` control scanning of existing objects and webhook failure behaviour respectively.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-limits
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Audit   # switch to Enforce after burn-in
  rules:
  - name: check-limits
    match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}]}
    validate:
      message: "CPU and memory limits are required"
      pattern: {spec: {containers: [{resources: {limits: {cpu: "?*", memory: "?*"}}}]}}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["Pod create request"] --> W["Kyverno admission webhook"]
    W -->|"Audit"| A["Admit and write PolicyReport"]
    W -->|"Enforce"| E["Reject with message"]
    A --> D["Team reviews violations"]

prompt: A vCluster (virtual cluster) requires its own dedicated worker nodes, separate from the host cluster, in order to run tenant workloads.
explanation: vCluster runs a virtual control plane (API server, controller manager, datastore) inside a namespace of the host cluster, and a syncer copies low-level resources such as Pods into that host namespace. Tenant Pods are therefore scheduled on the host cluster's existing nodes; no dedicated nodes are needed, which is what makes vCluster a cheap multi-tenancy option.
example:
vcluster create team-a --namespace team-a   # control plane runs as pods in ns team-a
vcluster connect team-a
kubectl get pods -A                          # tenant sees only its own virtual cluster
# on the host: kubectl get pods -n team-a  shows synced tenant pods + vcluster control plane
diagram:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Host["Host cluster"]
        NS["Namespace team-a"]
        NS --> CP["Virtual API server and datastore"]
        NS --> SY["Syncer"]
        SY -->|"syncs pods into host ns"| N["Shared host nodes"]
    end
    T["Tenant kubectl"] --> CP

prompt: In a shared multi-tenant cluster, a platform team wants to cap the total CPU and memory that all Pods in the `team-a` namespace may request, so one team cannot starve others. Which Kubernetes object should they create?
options: A `ResourceQuota` in the `team-a` namespace
A `LimitRange` in the `team-a` namespace
A `NetworkPolicy` in the `team-a` namespace
A `PriorityClass` assigned to team-a Pods
optionNotes: Correct. A ResourceQuota constrains aggregate resource consumption (requests, limits, object counts) across an entire namespace.
A LimitRange sets per-Pod or per-container defaults and min/max values; it does not cap the namespace total.
NetworkPolicy controls traffic flow, not compute resources.
PriorityClass influences scheduling and preemption order but does not limit consumption.
explanation: ResourceQuota is the namespace-level aggregate cap: it tracks the sum of requests and limits and rejects new Pods that would exceed it. LimitRange complements it by setting per-container defaults and bounds (and is needed so every Pod declares requests when a quota is present).
example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 64Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    pods: "200"
kubectl describe quota -n team-a
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["New Pod in team-a"] --> Q["ResourceQuota admission check"]
    Q -->|"sum within hard limits"| OK["Scheduled"]
    Q -->|"would exceed"| REJ["Rejected 403"]
    LR["LimitRange"] -->|"injects default requests"| P

prompt: A platform team publishes an SLO of 99.9% successful requests over 30 days for its internal build service. What does the resulting error budget represent?
options: The 0.1% of requests that may fail in the window before the SLO is breached, used to decide how much risk (such as releases) to accept
The monetary compensation owed to users when the service fails
The number of on-call engineers needed to keep the service within target
The maximum CPU the service may consume before autoscaling triggers
optionNotes: Correct. The error budget is 100% minus the SLO target; while budget remains, teams can ship changes, and when it is exhausted they prioritise reliability work.
Financial penalties belong to SLAs (contracts), not SLOs or error budgets.
Staffing is not what an error budget measures.
Resource consumption is unrelated to the SLO's success-rate objective.
explanation: An SLO of 99.9% leaves an error budget of 0.1% of requests (about 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days). Error budgets turn reliability into a shared, data-driven policy: spend budget on velocity while it lasts, freeze risky changes when it runs out. SLAs, staffing and resource limits are different concepts.
example:
# Sloth-style SLO definition
slos:
- name: build-api-availability
  objective: 99.9
  sli:
    events:
      error_query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="build-api",code=~"5.."}[{{.window}}]))
      total_query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="build-api"}[{{.window}}]))
# error budget = 0.1% of requests per 30d
diagram:
flowchart LR
    SLI["SLI: success ratio"] --> SLO["SLO: 99.9 percent over 30d"]
    SLO --> EB["Error budget: 0.1 percent"]
    EB -->|"budget left"| SHIP["Ship features"]
    EB -->|"budget spent"| FREEZE["Reliability work first"]
    BR["Burn-rate alert"] -.-> EB

prompt: The best indicator of an internal platform's success is the number of features the platform team has shipped in the last quarter.
explanation: Shipping features is an output, not an outcome. Platform success is measured by adoption (how many teams voluntarily use the golden paths), developer experience and satisfaction, time-to-first-deploy or onboarding time, and downstream delivery metrics such as DORA. A platform with many unused features has failed as a product.
example:
# outcome metrics on a platform dashboard
platform_active_teams / total_teams          # adoption
p50 time_to_first_prod_deploy                  # onboarding speed
quarterly developer satisfaction score        # DX
DORA metrics for teams on vs off the platform  # impact
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["Features shipped"] -.->|"output only"| X["Weak signal"]
    A["Adoption rate"] --> S["Platform success"]
    D["Developer satisfaction"] --> S
    T["Time to first deploy"] --> S
    DO["DORA metrics"] --> S

prompt: A platform team builds a Crossplane API so application teams can request a PostgreSQL database from their own namespace with `kubectl apply`, without seeing cloud-provider details. Which Crossplane object should developers create?
options: A namespaced Claim generated from the XRD's `claimNames`
The cluster-scoped Composite Resource (XR) directly
A `Composition` with the provider-specific managed resources
A `ProviderConfig` pointing at their cloud credentials
optionNotes: Correct. When an XRD declares `claimNames`, Crossplane generates a namespaced Claim kind; developers create it in their namespace and Crossplane binds it to a cluster-scoped XR that the Composition satisfies.
XRs are cluster-scoped and usually reserved for platform operators; exposing them directly to tenants breaks namespace isolation.
The Composition is the platform team's implementation detail mapping the XR to managed resources; developers should not author it.
ProviderConfig holds cloud credentials and is managed by the platform team, not per-request by developers.
explanation: Crossplane's abstraction stack is XRD (schema) -> Composition (implementation) -> XR (cluster-scoped instance) -> Claim (namespaced, developer-facing proxy). Claims are the intended self-service interface because they are namespaced and hide the managed resources. Note that Crossplane v2 also allows namespaced XRs directly, but the Claim remains the classic developer-facing pattern.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    DEV["Developer"] -->|"kubectl apply"| C["Claim PostgreSQL in namespace"]
    C -->|"binds"| XR["XR XPostgreSQL cluster-scoped"]
    XRD["XRD schema"] -.-> XR
    XR -->|"selects"| COMP["Composition"]
    COMP --> MR["Managed resources e.g. RDS instance"]

prompt: In Cluster API, which resource kind manages a set of worker `Machine` objects and performs rolling updates when its template changes, analogous to a Kubernetes Deployment?
explanation: Cluster API models worker nodes with a Deployment-like hierarchy: a `MachineDeployment` owns `MachineSet`s, which own `Machine`s, and a change to the infrastructure or bootstrap template triggers a rolling replacement of Machines. Control plane nodes are instead managed by `KubeadmControlPlane` (or another control plane provider).
example:
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: MachineDeployment
metadata:
  name: tenant-1-md-0
spec:
  clusterName: tenant-1
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      version: v1.31.4          # bump -> rolling node replacement
      bootstrap: {configRef: {kind: KubeadmConfigTemplate, name: tenant-1-md-0}}
      infrastructureRef: {kind: AWSMachineTemplate, name: tenant-1-md-0}
diagram:
flowchart TD
    CL["Cluster"] --> KCP["KubeadmControlPlane"]
    CL --> MD["MachineDeployment"]
    MD --> MS["MachineSet"]
    MS --> M1["Machine"]
    MS --> M2["Machine"]
    M1 --> INF["Infra provider VM"]

prompt: A platform team adopts the Kubernetes Gateway API with its role-oriented design. Application developers should be able to publish their own HTTP paths and hostnames without touching shared load balancer infrastructure. Which resource should the platform delegate to application developers?
options: `HTTPRoute`
`Gateway`
`GatewayClass`
`Ingress`
optionNotes: Correct. HTTPRoute is the namespaced, application-developer-facing resource that declares hostnames, matches and backends and attaches to a Gateway via `parentRefs`.
Gateway represents the shared listener/load balancer and is owned by the cluster operator (platform team).
GatewayClass is cluster-scoped and defined by the infrastructure provider or controller vendor.
Ingress is the older API that the Gateway API is designed to supersede; it is not part of the Gateway API role model.
explanation: Gateway API separates personas: infrastructure provider (GatewayClass), cluster operator (Gateway) and application developer (HTTPRoute and other Route kinds). Routes attach to Gateways under the Gateway's `allowedRoutes` policy, so developers get self-service routing while the platform team keeps control of the shared entry point.
example:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: orders, namespace: team-orders}
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: shared-gw
    namespace: platform-ingress   # Gateway owned by platform team
  hostnames: ["orders.example.com"]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]
    backendRefs: [{name: orders-svc, port: 8080}]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    IP["Infra provider"] --> GC["GatewayClass"]
    OP["Platform team"] --> GW["Gateway shared-gw"]
    GC --> GW
    DEV["App developer"] --> HR["HTTPRoute"]
    HR -->|"parentRefs"| GW
    HR --> SVC["Service orders-svc"]

prompt: Which custom resource kinds are installed by Argo Rollouts to implement progressive delivery? (Select all that apply.)
options: `Rollout`
`AnalysisTemplate`
`Experiment`
`Canary`
`TrafficSplit`
`Deployment`
optionNotes: `Rollout` is the Argo Rollouts drop-in replacement for Deployment that adds canary and blue-green strategies.
`AnalysisTemplate` (and `ClusterAnalysisTemplate`) define metric queries and success conditions used to gate or roll back a rollout automatically.
`Experiment` runs one or more ephemeral ReplicaSets for a set duration to compare versions, optionally with analysis.
There is no `Canary` CRD; canary is a strategy configured under `Rollout.spec.strategy.canary`.
`TrafficSplit` is an SMI (Service Mesh Interface) resource that Argo Rollouts can drive as a traffic router, but it is not a CRD shipped by Argo Rollouts.
`Deployment` is a core Kubernetes workload API, not an Argo Rollouts CRD (though a Rollout can reference one via `workloadRef`).
explanation: Argo Rollouts installs the `Rollout`, `AnalysisTemplate`, `ClusterAnalysisTemplate`, `AnalysisRun` and `Experiment` CRDs. Canary and blue-green are strategies inside a Rollout, not kinds. `TrafficSplit` belongs to SMI and `Deployment` to core Kubernetes.
example:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - analysis:
          templates: [{templateName: success-rate}]   # AnalysisTemplate
      - setWeight: 50
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout web --watch
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["Rollout canary strategy"] -->|"10 percent"| C["Canary ReplicaSet"]
    R --> S["Stable ReplicaSet"]
    R -->|"step analysis"| AR["AnalysisRun from AnalysisTemplate"]
    AR -->|"metrics from Prometheus"| P["Prometheus"]
    AR -->|"pass"| PROMOTE["Promote"]
    AR -->|"fail"| ABORT["Abort and rollback"]

prompt: A platform team runs HashiCorp Vault and wants every namespace to be able to sync secrets from it using External Secrets Operator (ESO), while keeping the Vault connection configuration defined once by the platform team. Which ESO resource should they create?
options: A `ClusterSecretStore`
A `SecretStore` in each namespace
A `ClusterExternalSecret`
A `PushSecret`
optionNotes: Correct. ClusterSecretStore is cluster-scoped and defines the backend (Vault address, auth) once; ExternalSecrets in any namespace can reference it with `secretStoreRef.kind: ClusterSecretStore`.
A namespaced SecretStore would require duplicating the Vault configuration in every namespace.
ClusterExternalSecret fans out one ExternalSecret definition to multiple namespaces; it does not define the backend connection.
PushSecret pushes a Kubernetes Secret out to the provider, the reverse direction of what is needed.
explanation: ESO separates the store (where and how to reach the provider) from the ExternalSecret (which keys to fetch and what Secret to create). A cluster-scoped `ClusterSecretStore` lets the platform team define the Vault connection once and optionally restrict which namespaces may use it via `conditions`. `SecretStore` is namespaced, `ClusterExternalSecret` templates ExternalSecrets across namespaces, and `PushSecret` writes secrets upstream.
example:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: vault}
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: https://vault.platform.svc:8200
      path: kv
      version: v2
      auth: {kubernetes: {mountPath: kubernetes, role: eso}}
---
kind: ExternalSecret
spec:
  secretStoreRef: {name: vault, kind: ClusterSecretStore}
  data: [{secretKey: password, remoteRef: {key: orders/db, property: password}}]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CSS["ClusterSecretStore vault"] -->|"k8s auth"| V["Vault KV"]
    ES["ExternalSecret in team-orders"] -->|"secretStoreRef"| CSS
    ESO["ESO controller"] -->|"reconciles"| ES
    ESO -->|"creates"| S["Secret orders-db"]
    POD["Pod"] -->|"mounts"| S

prompt: A platform team runs the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet to receive OTLP traces from tenant workloads. They want every span automatically tagged with the Kubernetes namespace, pod name and deployment name before export, without changing application code. Which Collector component provides this?
options: The `k8sattributes` processor
The `otlp` receiver
The `resourcedetection` exporter
The `kubeletstats` receiver
optionNotes: Correct. The `k8sattributes` processor looks up the Pod that emitted the telemetry (by IP or connection metadata) via the Kubernetes API and adds resource attributes such as `k8s.namespace.name`, `k8s.pod.name` and `k8s.deployment.name`.
The `otlp` receiver only accepts OTLP data over gRPC/HTTP; it does not enrich it.
`resourcedetection` is a processor (not an exporter) that detects host or cloud attributes; it does not resolve per-Pod Kubernetes metadata.
`kubeletstats` scrapes node and Pod metrics from the kubelet; it does not touch trace spans.
explanation: Collector pipelines are receivers -> processors -> exporters. Enrichment is a processor job, and `k8sattributes` is the one that associates telemetry with its source Pod and attaches Kubernetes metadata, which is essential for a multi-tenant platform to attribute traces to teams. The Collector needs RBAC to list Pods and ReplicaSets for this to work.
example:
processors:
  k8sattributes:
    passthrough: false
    extract:
      metadata: [k8s.namespace.name, k8s.pod.name, k8s.deployment.name]
    pod_association:
    - sources: [{from: connection}]
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    APP["Tenant app OTLP"] --> R["otlp receiver"]
    R --> K8S["k8sattributes processor"]
    API["Kubernetes API pods and replicasets"] -.->|"metadata lookup"| K8S
    K8S --> B["batch processor"]
    B --> E["otlp exporter"]
    E --> T["Tracing backend"]

prompt: OpenCost and Kubecost allocate the CPU and memory cost of a container using the larger of its resource request and its actual usage, so an over-requested but idle container is still charged for what it reserved.
explanation: OpenCost's allocation model charges `max(request, usage)` for CPU and RAM per container. This reflects that a request reserves capacity other workloads cannot use, and it is the mechanism that surfaces over-provisioning as a cost line item. Platform teams use this to show tenants the savings from right-sizing requests.
example:
# OpenCost allocation API, cost per namespace over 7 days
curl -s 'http://opencost.opencost:9090/allocation?window=7d&aggregate=namespace' | jq '.data[0][] | {name, cpuCost, ramCost, totalCost}'
# reduce cost: lower requests toward observed usage, or use a VPA recommendation
diagram:
flowchart LR
    REQ["request 2 CPU"] --> MAX["max of request and usage"]
    USE["usage 0.3 CPU"] --> MAX
    MAX -->|"2 CPU"| PRICE["x node CPU hourly price"]
    PRICE --> COST["container cost"]
    COST -->|"aggregate by namespace label"| SHOW["Showback per team"]

prompt: Give the Sigstore `cosign` subcommand that a CI pipeline runs to attach a signature to a container image in a registry (write the command and subcommand, without flags).
explanation: `cosign sign` signs an image (ideally referenced by digest) and pushes the signature to the registry alongside the image as an OCI artifact. In keyless mode it uses an OIDC identity from the CI provider and records the signing event in the Rekor transparency log; admission controllers such as Kyverno `verifyImages` or the Sigstore policy-controller then verify with `cosign verify` semantics before Pods run.
example:
# keyless signing in CI (GitHub Actions OIDC)
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/orders@sha256:3f1c...
# attach an SBOM as an attestation
syft ghcr.io/acme/orders@sha256:3f1c... -o spdx-json > sbom.json
cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.json --type spdxjson ghcr.io/acme/orders@sha256:3f1c...
# verify

prompt: A platform team must autoscale a queue-consumer Deployment based on the number of messages in a RabbitMQ queue, and it must scale all the way down to zero replicas when the queue is empty. Which approach satisfies both requirements?
options: A KEDA `ScaledObject` with a `rabbitmq` trigger
A `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` using a `Pods` metric with `minReplicas: 0`
A `VerticalPodAutoscaler` in `Auto` mode
A Cluster Autoscaler configured with a minimum node count of zero
optionNotes: Correct. KEDA provides event-source scalers (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS, Prometheus and more) and can scale a workload from 0 to 1 itself, then hands 1..N scaling to an HPA it manages.
A standard HPA cannot scale to zero by default (`minReplicas` must be at least 1 unless the alpha `HPAScaleToZero` feature gate is enabled), and it has no built-in RabbitMQ metric source.
VPA adjusts CPU/memory requests of Pods; it does not change replica counts.
Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, not Deployments; it cannot react to queue depth.
explanation: KEDA is the standard platform building block for event-driven autoscaling. A ScaledObject references the target Deployment and a trigger; KEDA activates the workload from zero when the queue has messages and creates an HPA that uses KEDA's external metrics for further scaling. HPA alone lacks scale-to-zero and queue-aware metrics; VPA and Cluster Autoscaler address different dimensions.
example:
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: {name: orders-consumer}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {name: orders-consumer}
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 30
  cooldownPeriod: 120
  triggers:
  - type: rabbitmq
    metadata: {queueName: orders, mode: QueueLength, value: "20", hostFromEnv: RABBITMQ_URL}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    Q["RabbitMQ queue length"] --> K["KEDA operator"]
    K -->|"0 to 1 activation"| D["Deployment orders-consumer"]
    K -->|"external metrics"| H["HPA managed by KEDA"]
    H -->|"1 to N"| D
    Q -->|"empty"| Z["scale to zero"]

prompt: A platform team asks tenants to define `PodDisruptionBudget`s so node upgrades do not take services down. Which statements about PDBs are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: A PDB only limits voluntary disruptions performed through the Eviction API, such as `kubectl drain`
`minAvailable` and `maxUnavailable` cannot both be set in the same PDB
A PDB prevents the kubelet from OOM-killing a container that exceeds its memory limit
`kubectl drain` blocks or retries evictions that would violate a matching PDB
A PDB stops a Deployment from being scaled down below `minAvailable` replicas
optionNotes: Correct. PDBs are consulted by the Eviction API, which drain, cluster autoscaler node scale-down and descheduler use; they do not cover involuntary disruptions like hardware failure.
Correct. The API rejects a PDB that specifies both fields; exactly one must be used (as an integer or percentage).
Incorrect. OOM kills, node crashes and kernel panics are involuntary disruptions that a PDB cannot prevent.
Correct. Drain uses the Eviction API, so evictions that would breach the budget return 429 and drain waits and retries until they are allowed.
Incorrect. Scaling a Deployment changes the desired replica count directly and is not an eviction, so the PDB is not consulted.
explanation: PodDisruptionBudgets protect against voluntary disruptions via the Eviction API: drain, node autoscaler scale-down and similar tools honour them, and evictions that would exceed the budget are refused (HTTP 429) until safe. They do not defend against involuntary events such as OOM kills or node failures, and they do not interfere with a controller deliberately scaling replicas. `minAvailable` and `maxUnavailable` are mutually exclusive.
example:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: {name: orders-pdb, namespace: team-orders}
spec:
  minAvailable: 2          # or maxUnavailable: 25%  (not both)
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: orders}
kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data   # waits on PDB
diagram:
flowchart LR
    DR["kubectl drain or autoscaler"] -->|"Eviction API"| EV["Eviction check"]
    PDB["PDB minAvailable 2"] --> EV
    EV -->|"budget ok"| EVICT["Pod evicted"]
    EV -->|"would breach"| WAIT["429 retry later"]
    OOM["OOM kill or node crash"] -.->|"not covered"| PDB

prompt: A platform team maintains ten Helm charts for different service archetypes and wants to share common named templates (labels, probes, security context) across all of them from one versioned source, without that shared package being installable on its own. Which Helm construct should they use?
options: A library chart with `type: library` added as a dependency
A subchart with `type: application` and `condition: false`
A `values.yaml` file shared through a symlink
A Helm plugin that injects templates at render time
optionNotes: Correct. Library charts declare `type: library` in `Chart.yaml`, contain only named templates (`define`) and helpers, cannot be installed directly, and are consumed as a dependency by application charts.
An application subchart renders its own resources and can be installed on its own; disabling it with a condition does not make its templates reusable.
Values files carry configuration, not templates, and symlinks do not version or package anything.
Helm plugins extend the CLI; they are not the mechanism for sharing chart templates.
explanation: Helm 3 introduced library charts precisely for platform teams: a `type: library` chart packages reusable named templates that other charts include with `{{ include "lib.labels" . }}` after listing it under `dependencies`. Helm refuses to install a library chart directly, which keeps the shared logic from being deployed by accident.

# platform-lib/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: platform-lib
type: library
version: 1.4.0
# app chart Chart.yaml
dependencies:
- name: platform-lib
  version: 1.4.0
  repository: oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts
# app template: {{ include "platform-lib.securityContext" . }}

    LIB["Library chart platform-lib type library"] -->|"dependency"| A["Chart go-service"]
    LIB -->|"dependency"| B["Chart java-service"]
    A -->|"include named templates"| RA["Rendered manifests"]
    B -->|"include named templates"| RB["Rendered manifests"]
    LIB -.->|"helm install refused"| X["Not installable alone"]

prompt: An enabling team pairs with a stream-aligned team for six weeks to help it adopt distributed tracing, then steps away once the team is self-sufficient. In Team Topologies terms, which interaction mode is this?

X-as-a-Service
Facilitating
Ticket-driven hand-off

Correct. Facilitating is the mode where one team (typically an enabling team) helps another learn a capability, with the explicit goal of making itself unnecessary.

explanation: Team Topologies defines three interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating. Enabling teams mostly use facilitating: they coach a stream-aligned team through a capability gap for a bounded period and then disengage.

Create a `ProviderConfig` in each team namespace
Grant teams `create` on the composite resource with a `ClusterRole`
Add a `Composition` per namespace

prompt: A platform team wants Crossplane to bring an existing, hand-built RDS instance under observation so its status appears in the cluster, but Crossplane must never modify or delete it. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Set the `crossplane.io/external-name` annotation to the instance identifier and `managementPolicies: ["Observe"]`
Set `deletionPolicy: Orphan` and leave `spec.forProvider` empty
Apply the managed resource with `kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts`
Set `managementPolicies: ["*"]` and copy every attribute of the instance into `spec.forProvider`
optionNotes: Correct. The external-name annotation tells the provider which real resource to look at, and the `Observe` management policy makes Crossplane read-only for that resource.
`deletionPolicy: Orphan` only prevents deletion; Crossplane would still try to create or update the resource to match `spec.forProvider`.
Server-side apply affects how the Kubernetes object is written and has nothing to do with the provider's behaviour towards the cloud resource.
`*` is the default full-management policy; any drift between the spec and reality would be corrected by Crossplane, which the team wants to avoid.
explanation: Managed resources support `managementPolicies` (Observe, Create, Update, Delete, LateInitialize, or `*`). Combining the `crossplane.io/external-name` annotation with `Observe` imports an existing resource in read-only mode; adding `Update` later lets the team take control incrementally.
example:
apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
kind: Instance
metadata:
  name: legacy-orders-db
  annotations:
    crossplane.io/external-name: orders-prod-01
spec:
  managementPolicies: ["Observe"]
  forProvider:
    region: eu-west-1
  providerConfigRef:
    name: aws-prod

    P -->|"describe"| RDS["Existing RDS orders-prod-01"]
    RDS -->|"status.atProvider"| MR

prompt: A developer writes a Score workload file that declares `resources.db.type: postgres` and injects `${resources.db.host}` into an environment variable. Who or what turns that abstract resource into a real database?

Kubernetes automatically creates a StatefulSet named `db` when the workload is applied
The container image must bundle a PostgreSQL server for the placeholder to resolve
The developer must add the connection string under `resources.db.params` before deploying

prompt: A platform team runs the Hierarchical Namespace Controller (HNC). A team lead with admin rights only in namespace `team-a` runs `kubectl hns create team-a-dev -n team-a`. What happens?
options: A `SubnamespaceAnchor` is created in `team-a`, HNC creates namespace `team-a-dev` as its child, and RoleBindings from `team-a` propagate into it
The command fails because creating namespaces always needs cluster-admin
A vCluster named `team-a-dev` is started inside `team-a`
Namespace `team-a-dev` is created but stays isolated with no inherited RBAC

HNC creates ordinary Kubernetes namespaces, not virtual clusters.
Propagation of RBAC and other configured kinds from the parent is the whole point of the hierarchy.

└── [s] team-a-dev

prompt: A platform team writes an OPA Gatekeeper `ConstraintTemplate` requiring an `owner` label on every Deployment. They want violations reported in the audit results and in `kubectl` warnings first, and only block requests after teams have had time to fix existing workloads. What should they set on the `Constraint`?

`spec.validationFailureAction: Audit` now, switching to `Enforce` later
Start Gatekeeper with `--disable-admission` until the cleanup is done
Leave `enforcementAction` at its default and rely on the audit controller only
optionNotes: Correct. `dryrun` records violations in the audit status without rejecting requests; `warn` additionally returns an admission warning to the client. Both let the team measure and communicate before flipping to `deny`.
`validationFailureAction` is Kyverno's field, not Gatekeeper's.
Disabling the admission webhook removes every constraint, including ones that must stay enforced.
The default `enforcementAction` is `deny`, so this would immediately block non-compliant Deployments.
explanation: Gatekeeper constraints support `enforcementAction` values `deny` (default), `dryrun` and `warn`. Audit periodically scans existing resources regardless of the action, so `dryrun` or `warn` gives a full picture of violations before enforcement starts.

apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: deployments-must-have-owner
spec:
  enforcementAction: warn
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        kinds: ["Deployment"]
  parameters:
    labels: ["owner"]

    CT["ConstraintTemplate (Rego)"] --> C["Constraint enforcementAction: warn"]
    REQ["Deployment without owner"] --> WH["Admission webhook"]

    AUD["Audit controller"] -->|"status.violations"| C
    C -.->|"later: deny"| WH

prompt: Which of the following are rule types that can appear inside a Kyverno `ClusterPolicy` rule? (Select all that apply.)
options: validate
mutate
generate
verifyImages
enforce
alert
optionNotes: Correct. `validate` rules accept or reject resources using a pattern, deny condition or CEL expression.
Correct. `mutate` rules patch resources on admission (or existing resources with `targets`).
Correct. `generate` rules create additional resources, such as a default NetworkPolicy when a Namespace appears.
Correct. `verifyImages` rules check image signatures and attestations, typically with Sigstore cosign or Notary.
`Enforce` is a value of `validationFailureAction` (alongside `Audit`), not a rule type.
Kyverno surfaces results through PolicyReports; there is no `alert` rule type.
explanation: A Kyverno rule declares exactly one of `validate`, `mutate`, `generate` or `verifyImages`. Cleanup is handled by a separate `ClusterCleanupPolicy` kind, and enforcement mode is a policy-level setting rather than a rule type.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-owner-label
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Audit
  rules:
    - name: check-owner
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Deployment"]
      validate:
        message: "label owner is required"
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              owner: "?*"
diagram:

prompt: A platform team uses a Kyverno `generate` rule to create a default-deny `NetworkPolicy` in every new Namespace and sets `synchronize: true`. A tenant later deletes the generated NetworkPolicy from their namespace. What happens?
options: Kyverno recreates the NetworkPolicy and keeps it in sync with the rule's definition
Nothing; generate rules only fire once when the trigger resource is created
The Namespace is deleted because the generated resource is its owner
Kyverno marks the Namespace as non-compliant in a PolicyReport but does not restore the object
optionNotes: Correct. With `synchronize: true` Kyverno treats the generated resource as managed: it is recreated if deleted and updated if the rule's data changes, and it is removed when the trigger is deleted.
That describes `synchronize: false`, where the generated object is created once and then left alone.
Ownership runs the other way: the generated resource is linked to the trigger, and deleting the child never deletes the parent.
PolicyReports are produced by validate rules; generate rules with synchronize actively reconcile instead of just reporting.
explanation: Kyverno `generate` rules create resources in response to a trigger (here, a Namespace). `synchronize: true` makes Kyverno continuously reconcile the generated resource so tenants cannot remove platform guardrails by deleting them.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-per-namespace
spec:
  rules:
    - name: generate-default-deny
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Namespace"]
      generate:
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: NetworkPolicy
        name: default-deny-ingress
        namespace: "{{request.object.metadata.name}}"
        synchronize: true
        data:
          spec:
            podSelector: {}
            policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    NS["New Namespace"] -->|"trigger"| KY["Kyverno generate rule"]
    KY -->|"creates"| NP["NetworkPolicy default-deny-ingress"]
    T["Tenant deletes NetworkPolicy"] --> KY
    KY -->|"synchronize: true, recreate"| NP

prompt: A Kyverno `verifyImages` rule only checks image signatures; with default settings it never modifies the Pod spec that is admitted.

This prevents a tag from being repointed after admission; set `mutateDigest: false` if the mutation is unwanted.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-acme-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:

      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/acme/*"]
          mutateDigest: true   # default
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: "https://github.com/acme/*"
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"

At the next scheduled nightly cleanup, regardless of PR state
Only when the developer runs a manual teardown command
Never; preview environments are promoted to become staging
optionNotes: Correct. Preview environments are tied to the lifetime of the change; closing or merging the PR triggers automatic teardown so cost and drift stay bounded.
Some platforms add a TTL as a safety net, but the primary trigger is the PR lifecycle, not a fixed nightly schedule.
Manual teardown is the failure mode ephemeral environments are designed to eliminate.
Preview environments are disposable; staging is a long-lived environment with its own promotion flow.
explanation: Ephemeral (preview) environments are created per branch or pull request and deleted automatically when the change is merged or abandoned. Tools such as the Argo CD ApplicationSet pull request generator or GitHub Actions environments implement this lifecycle.

Costs must be allocated with a consistent key such as namespace or a mandatory `team` label
Shared platform costs (monitoring, ingress, control plane) and idle capacity need an explicit distribution rule
Showback requires finance to issue an internal invoice to each team every month
Tenants who see their showback numbers are not expected to change behaviour until chargeback begins

Correct. Without a reliable allocation dimension, a large share of spend ends up unallocated and the report loses credibility.

The purpose of showback is to drive behaviour through visibility; many organisations never move to chargeback at all.

prompt: Six months after launching a golden-path CI/CD template, a platform team reviews adoption: only 4 of 22 services use it. Interviews reveal the template's pipeline takes 38 minutes end to end (mandatory full SAST scan, image rebuild on every commit, serial integration tests), while the teams' hand-rolled pipelines finish in 9 minutes. Several teams copied the template once and then stripped the slow stages. Leadership asks the platform team what to do next. Which response best fits a platform-as-a-product approach?
options: Treat the 38-minute pipeline as the product defect: profile the stages, cache and parallelise, move the full SAST scan to a nightly or merge-time job, and publish a measured target (for example under 10 minutes) before asking anyone to migrate
Ask leadership to mandate the golden path through an admission policy that blocks images not built by the template pipeline
Add a second, lighter template with SAST removed so teams can pick whichever they like
Leave the template as is; 38 minutes is the cost of compliance and the teams that stripped stages should be reported to security
optionNotes: Correct. Adoption is the signal that the product is worse than the alternative for its users. Fixing the real bottleneck and measuring it (lead time, pipeline duration) is how a platform earns adoption instead of demanding it.
A mandate would force teams onto a pipeline that is four times slower, which pushes the cost onto every stream-aligned team and typically produces workarounds and resentment rather than adoption.
Forking the template doubles maintenance and quietly drops the security control; the goal is one paved road that is both fast and compliant.
Blaming users for routing around a slow product ignores the evidence; the stripped stages show the template's shape, not the teams, is the problem.
explanation: When teams bypass a golden path, the paved road is losing to the dirt road on the metric developers actually feel: time to feedback. A product-minded platform team treats low adoption as a defect, instruments the pipeline, removes the slow stages from the inner loop (run heavy scans at merge or on a schedule), and sets a measurable target. Mandates and forks address the symptom, not the cause.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A["Adoption 4 of 22 services"] --> B["Interview users"]
    B --> C["Symptom: golden path 38 min vs 9 min DIY"]
    C --> D["Profile stages: SAST 15 min, build 11 min"]
    D --> E["Move SAST to merge-time, cache build, shard tests"]
    E --> F["Publish target under 10 min"]
    F --> G["Re-measure adoption"]

prompt: A five-person platform team owns the shared Kubernetes clusters for 30 product teams. Their Jira board shows 140 open tickets, median age 12 days, and 70% of them are variations of three requests: create a namespace with RBAC, add a DNS record and TLS certificate for a new service, and grant a team access to a cloud bucket. The team spends almost all its time executing these tickets by hand and has not shipped a platform improvement in two quarters. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Turn the three most common requests into self-service capabilities (for example a Backstage software template or a Crossplane claim) that validate input and provision automatically, then measure ticket volume drop
Hire two more platform engineers to work the queue down
Add a Jira SLA of 3 business days and an on-call rotation for ticket triage
Move the platform engineers into the product teams as embedded SREs so each team can do its own provisioning
optionNotes: Correct. A platform team that executes repetitive requests by hand has become a ticket queue; the fix is to encode those requests as self-service APIs so the team is removed from the critical path and gets time back for platform work.
More hands scale the queue linearly at best; demand from 30 teams will keep growing and the work is still manual.
An SLA makes the queue more predictable but does not shrink it; it formalises the platform team as a service desk.

Embedding removes the platform team entirely, spreads the same manual work across 30 teams, and loses the economies of a shared platform; Team Topologies would call this dissolving the platform rather than fixing it.
explanation: Team Topologies distinguishes a platform team, which offers capabilities as self-service via an API or portal (X-as-a-Service interaction), from a team that interacts by handling requests. When three request types make up 70% of a stagnant queue, turning them into templates or claims with validation removes the human from the loop. The success measure is the drop in tickets and the reclaimed platform engineering time.
example:
# Backstage software template that replaces the namespace ticket
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: k8s-namespace
  title: Request a Kubernetes namespace
spec:
  parameters:
    - required: [team, env]
      properties:
        team: {type: string, pattern: '^[a-z0-9-]{3,20}$'}
        env:  {type: string, enum: [dev, staging, prod]}
  steps:
    - id: pr
      action: publish:github:pull-request
      input:
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=acme&repo=platform-tenants
        branchName: ns-${{ parameters.team }}-${{ parameters.env }}
        title: Add namespace ${{ parameters.team }}-${{ parameters.env }}
# Argo CD applies the merged tenant manifest; no platform engineer in the loop.

flowchart LR
    T["140 tickets, 70% are 3 request types"] --> Q["Platform team as ticket queue"]
    Q --> S["Encode requests as self-service templates or claims"]
    S --> V["Input validation and policy in the template"]
    V --> A["Automated provisioning via GitOps"]
    A --> M["Measure: tickets down, platform time reclaimed"]

prompt: A developer applies a Crossplane claim `PostgreSQLInstance/orders-db` in namespace `orders`. Twenty minutes later `kubectl get postgresqlinstance -n orders` shows `SYNCED: True`, `READY: False`. The platform engineer runs `kubectl get managed` and sees `rdsinstance.rds.aws.upbound.io/orders-db-x7k2p  SYNCED: False  READY: False`. `kubectl describe` on that RDSInstance shows the condition `ReconcileError: cannot get AWS credentials: cannot get credentials secret: Secret "aws-creds" not found` in the `crossplane-system` namespace. The Composition and XRD are unchanged since last week, when other claims worked. What is the most likely root cause and fix?
options: The `ProviderConfig` the Composition references points to a credentials Secret that has been deleted or rotated under a new name; restore or re-create `aws-creds` in `crossplane-system` (or update `ProviderConfig.spec.credentials.secretRef`) and the managed resource will reconcile
The claim is in the wrong namespace; claims must be created in `crossplane-system` so the provider can read its credentials
The Composition's `compositeTypeRef` no longer matches the XRD, so the composite resource cannot be built; re-apply the Composition
The developer forgot `spec.writeConnectionSecretToRef`, so Crossplane cannot store the connection details and marks the claim not ready
optionNotes: Correct. The claim and composite resource were created (SYNCED True on the claim) and the managed RDSInstance was composed, but the provider cannot authenticate because the Secret named in the `ProviderConfig` is missing. Restoring the Secret lets the managed resource reconcile and readiness propagates back up to the claim.
Claims are namespaced and belong in the tenant namespace; the provider credentials live in `crossplane-system` regardless of where claims are created.
If `compositeTypeRef` were wrong the composite resource would not have been created and there would be no managed resource to show an AWS error.
A missing connection secret reference does not block provisioning; the RDSInstance would still become Ready, and the error text is explicitly about provider credentials.
explanation: A claim that is SYNCED but not READY means Crossplane accepted it and created the composite, and readiness is blocked further down. `kubectl get managed` finds the composed cloud resource, and its `ReconcileError` names the real problem: the provider's `ProviderConfig` references a credentials Secret that no longer exists, typically after a secret rotation or a namespace cleanup. Fixing the Secret or the `secretRef` unblocks the managed resource without touching the claim.
example:
$ kubectl get postgresqlinstance -n orders
NAME        SYNCED   READY   CONNECTION-SECRET   AGE
orders-db   True     False   orders-db-conn      21m

$ kubectl get managed
NAME                                             SYNCED   READY   EXTERNAL-NAME
rdsinstance.rds.aws.upbound.io/orders-db-x7k2p   False    False

$ kubectl describe rdsinstance orders-db-x7k2p | grep -A2 ReconcileError
  Reason:  ReconcileError
  Message: cannot get AWS credentials: cannot get credentials secret: Secret "aws-creds" not found

$ kubectl get providerconfig default -o jsonpath='{.spec.credentials.secretRef}'
{"key":"creds","name":"aws-creds","namespace":"crossplane-system"}
$ kubectl get secret -n crossplane-system aws-creds
Error from server (NotFound): secrets "aws-creds" not found

# Fix: restore the secret (for example via External Secrets) and watch reconcile
$ kubectl get managed -w
diagram:
flowchart TD
    C["Claim orders-db SYNCED True READY False"] --> X["Composite XPostgreSQLInstance"]
    X --> M["Managed RDSInstance SYNCED False"]
    M --> E["ReconcileError: credentials secret not found"]
    E --> P["ProviderConfig secretRef aws-creds"]
    P --> F["Restore Secret in crossplane-system"]
    F --> R["Managed becomes Ready, claim becomes Ready"]

prompt: A platform team flips a Kyverno `ClusterPolicy` named `require-run-as-nonroot` from `Audit` to `Enforce` at 09:30. By 09:45 alerts fire: cert-manager cannot renew certificates, the `kube-system` CoreDNS Deployment cannot roll out a replacement Pod after a node drain, and tenant deploys fail with `admission webhook "validate.kyverno.svc-fail" denied the request: ... validation error: Running as root is not allowed`. The team had only reviewed PolicyReports for the tenant namespaces before enforcing. Which actions are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
options: Immediately set the policy back to `validationFailureAction: Audit` to restore admission, then work from the PolicyReports
Add an `exclude` block (or a namespace selector) so `kube-system`, `cert-manager`, and other platform namespaces are out of scope for this policy before re-enforcing
Run `kyverno apply` against the manifests of every namespace, including system ones, in CI so violations are known before a policy is enforced
Delete the `kyverno-resource-validating-webhook-cfg` ValidatingWebhookConfiguration by hand to stop the blocking
Set `background: false` on the policy so it stops blocking admission
optionNotes: Correct. Returning to Audit is the fastest, lowest-risk rollback: resources are admitted again and the reports show exactly what still violates.
Correct. System and platform components that legitimately run as root must be excluded explicitly; the blast radius came from enforcing cluster-wide without scoping.
Correct. Testing policies against real manifests in CI (or reviewing PolicyReports for all namespaces, not just tenants) is how the gap would have been caught before enforcement.
Kyverno manages that webhook configuration and will re-create it within seconds; hand-deleting it also disables every other policy, which is a far larger change than rolling back one policy.
`background` only controls scanning of existing resources for reports; admission behaviour is governed by `validationFailureAction`, so this changes nothing about the outage.
explanation: The policy was enforced against the whole cluster while only tenant namespaces had been reviewed, so system workloads that run as root were blocked at admission. The safe sequence is roll back to Audit, scope the policy with `exclude` or namespace selectors, prove the policy against all manifests with `kyverno apply` or complete PolicyReports, then re-enforce. Deleting webhook configurations or changing `background` do not address admission behaviour.
example:
# Roll back
$ kubectl patch clusterpolicy require-run-as-nonroot --type merge \
    -p '{"spec":{"validationFailureAction":"Audit"}}'

# Scope the policy before enforcing again
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: run-as-non-root
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod]
      exclude:
        any:
          - resources:
              namespaces: [kube-system, cert-manager, kyverno, monitoring]

# Prove it in CI against rendered manifests
$ kyverno apply policies/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml --resource rendered/all-namespaces.yaml

# Check what is still failing cluster-wide
$ kubectl get policyreport -A | grep -v ' 0 '
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A["Policy set to Enforce cluster-wide"] --> B["System Pods denied: CoreDNS, cert-manager"]
    B --> C["Roll back to Audit"]
    C --> D["Review PolicyReports for all namespaces"]
    D --> E["Add exclude for platform namespaces"]
    E --> F["kyverno apply in CI"]
    F --> G["Re-enforce with known scope"]

prompt: On a shared cluster, tenants in namespace `analytics` report their batch jobs being `OOMKilled` and `Evicted` with `The node was low on resource: memory` even though the jobs set memory requests and limits. Investigation shows namespace `team-web` has a `ResourceQuota` capping total requests, but its Pods are created by a Helm chart that sets no `resources` at all, so each Pod counts as zero requests against the quota and the scheduler packs dozens of them onto the same nodes as the analytics jobs. Under load, `team-web` Pods consume real memory they never requested. Which change fixes the root cause with the least disruption?
options: Add a `LimitRange` to `team-web` (and by policy to every tenant namespace) that sets `defaultRequest` and `default` for CPU and memory, so Pods without explicit resources get requests the scheduler and quota can account for
Raise the memory requests on the `analytics` jobs so they reserve more headroom on the node
Move `team-web` to a dedicated node pool using `nodeSelector` and taints so its Pods never share nodes with `analytics`
Lower the `ResourceQuota` in `team-web` to `requests.memory: 4Gi` so fewer of its Pods can run
optionNotes: Correct. The scheduler and quota only see requests; Pods with none are invisible to both. A `LimitRange` injects default requests and limits at admission, so `team-web` Pods are accounted for, quota becomes meaningful, and node packing stops overcommitting memory. Existing Pods pick up defaults on their next restart.

Raising the victim's requests does not stop the neighbour from consuming unrequested memory; the node is still overcommitted and the eviction ordering still targets whoever bursts above request first.
A dedicated pool isolates this one tenant but costs capacity and leaves the underlying problem (unrequested Pods) to recur with the next tenant that omits resources.
Quota is measured in requests; since these Pods request zero, lowering the quota to 4Gi still admits an unlimited number of them.
explanation: A `ResourceQuota` only counts declared requests, so Pods with no `resources` stanza consume real memory the scheduler never reserved: the classic noisy neighbour on a shared cluster. A `LimitRange` with `defaultRequest` and `default` values is the admission-time control that gives every Pod a request and limit, making quota and bin-packing accurate. Many platform teams generate one in every tenant namespace with Kyverno so a chart can never opt out.
example:
# Confirm the neighbour's Pods request nothing
$ kubectl get pods -n team-web -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.memory'
NAME                 REQ
web-7c9f5d8b6-2xk4q  <none>
web-7c9f5d8b6-9plz2  <none>

$ kubectl describe node ip-10-0-3-41 | grep -A3 'Allocated resources'
  memory  6200Mi (39%)   # requests look fine, but actual usage is 15.2Gi of 16Gi

# Fix
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: team-web
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest: {cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi}
      default:        {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
      max:            {cpu: "4",  memory: 8Gi}
diagram:
flowchart TD
    H["team-web chart sets no resources"] --> Z["Pods request 0, quota counts 0"]
    Z --> S["Scheduler packs many Pods per node"]
    S --> N["Node memory pressure"]
    N --> V["analytics jobs Evicted or OOMKilled"]
    L["LimitRange defaultRequest and default"] --> Z2["Every Pod gets requests at admission"]
    Z2 --> Q["Quota and bin-packing become accurate"]

prompt: A platform team replaces its deployment tooling with a new GitOps-based flow. team-payments   41%   # was 5%: new flow skips canary stage the old pipeline had

...

    C --> R["Change failure rate 6% to 19%"]

prompt: A platform team rolls out OpenCost for showback. The first monthly report attributes 43% of cluster spend to `__unallocated__` when aggregated by the `team` label, because many Deployments were created before the label convention existed and some Helm charts never set it. Finance wants accurate numbers next month. What is the best next step?
options: Enforce the `team` label at admission (for example a Kyverno policy that requires it on new workloads) and run a one-off pass to backfill the label on existing Deployments, then re-run the report
Change the OpenCost aggregation from `label:team` to `namespace` and tell finance to map namespaces to teams manually
Split the unallocated cost evenly across all teams so the totals add up
Increase the OpenCost scrape interval so more cost samples carry a label
optionNotes: Correct. Missing labels are a data-quality problem at the source; an admission policy prevents new gaps and a backfill closes the existing ones, so the next report allocates cost to the right owners.
Namespace aggregation only works if every namespace maps cleanly to one team, which is rarely true on shared clusters, and it still leaves the metadata gap unfixed.
Even spreading is arbitrary and hides the real cost drivers; teams cannot act on numbers that are not theirs.
Scrape interval affects sample resolution, not whether a workload has a label; the missing metadata is on the Kubernetes objects.
explanation: Cost allocation tools can only attribute spend to labels that exist on the workloads. A large `__unallocated__` bucket means the labelling convention is not enforced; the durable fix is to require the label at admission and backfill it on existing objects so both new and old workloads carry an owner.
example:
# Find the offenders
$ kubectl get deploy -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.labels.team==null) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' | head

# Prevent new gaps
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: team-label
      match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet, CronJob]}}]}
      validate:
        message: "label team is required for cost allocation"
        pattern: {metadata: {labels: {team: "?*"}}}

# Backfill (label the pod template too so OpenCost sees it on Pods)
$ kubectl -n checkout label deploy/cart team=payments
$ kubectl -n checkout patch deploy/cart -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"labels":{"team":"payments"}}}}}'
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["OpenCost report: 43% unallocated"] --> W["Workloads missing team label"]
    W --> P["Kyverno policy requires label on new workloads"]
    W --> B["Backfill label on existing Deployments"]
    P --> N["Next report allocates cost per team"]
    B --> N

prompt: A platform team owns a Crossplane XRD `xapps.platform.example.com` whose `v1alpha1` schema is used by 60 claims across 25 teams. They need to ship a `v1beta1` that renames `spec.parameters.size` to `spec.parameters.tier` and changes its allowed values. Last time they changed the schema in place, every existing claim went `Ready: False` with a validation error and three teams paged the platform on-call. Which practices make this rollout safe? (Select all that apply.)

Mark `v1alpha1` with `deprecated: true` and a `deprecationWarning` so `kubectl` prints a warning pointing users to `v1beta1`

explanation: Platform APIs are consumed like any Kubernetes API, so breaking changes need versioning rather than in-place edits. Adding a new served version, deprecating the old one with a warning, and removing it only after a communicated window and evidence of zero usage lets 25 teams migrate without a flag day. Note that Crossplane XRDs currently expect a single referenceable version, so the Composition targets the new version while the old one remains served for reads and updates.
example:
apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: xapps.platform.example.com
spec:
  group: platform.example.com
  names: {kind: XApp, plural: xapps}
  claimNames: {kind: App, plural: apps}
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      referenceable: false
      deprecated: true
      deprecationWarning: "platform.example.com/v1alpha1 App is deprecated; migrate to v1beta1 (parameters.size -> parameters.tier) before 2026-12-01"
      schema: {openAPIV3Schema: {...}}
    - name: v1beta1
      served: true
      referenceable: true
      schema: {openAPIV3Schema: {...}}

# Before removal: confirm nobody still writes v1alpha1
$ kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep 'apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis{group="platform.example.com"'
